newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tension palpable as Russian cosmonauts return.
newsitem.headline: Tension palpable as Russian cosmonauts return.

text.p: The tension was palpable at Mission Control on Thursday as Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin made their way to Earth after one of the toughest space missions ever.

"Everything will be okay, don't worry and make sure you eat something," a Mission Control official told the pair in the last seconds before they started the engines of their Soyuz spacecraft and undocked from the Mir space station.
A space expert said the two were supposed to eat lots of starch to boost their strength for the 400 km (250 mile) journey to their landing site on the steppes of Kazakhstan.
The stress came across in the voices of the operators during regular radio exchanges with Soyuz, conducted from a big hall at Mission Control in the town of Korolyov near Moscow.
About 30 operators gathered in front of banks of computers and three screens during the half-hourly exchanges. They scattered to separate rooms in the intervals to make extra calculations.
The largest screen, switched off like the others in the breaks between exchanges, showed a map of the world with a point of light imitating the flight of the Mir space station.
To one side, two screens carried graphics of Soyuz undocking from Mir and floating away towards Earth and another contained information about the systems working on Mir and Soyuz.
After undocking, operators began working with Soyuz in another hall, away from the prying eyes and camera lenses of a horde of journalists gathered to record the descent.
Tsibliyev and flight engineer Lazutkin earlier hugged their two Russian replacements and NASA astronaut Michael Foale and waved for the cameras as they floated into the airlock to Soyuz.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said in a live broadcast from Mir shown on television screens. "We are leaving. See you on Earth."
A Mission Control operator told Tsibliyev and Lazutkin: "Thank you for the job you've done. Happy landing."

Thousands of miles away in the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan, top space officials had already gathered in the town of Dzhezkazgan, ready to fly out to the landing site in the middle of the steppe to greet the returning crew.

Once a huge orange parachute opens to slow the capsule after it enters the Earth's atmosphere, it will take just 15 minutes to fall to the ground. Eight rescue helicopters will be in the air near the spot where the capsule is due to land.

"The cosmonauts will be helped out of the capsule. They will undergo medical checks immediately in a tent, then they will take a helicopter to Dzhezkazgan," said Pyotr Klimuk, head of the Cosmonauts' Training Centre, Star City.
"The main thing is to judge their ability to be transported," said Vladimir Nikulin, Star City's main surgeon.
From there they will travel by plane to the Chkalovsky military airbase near Moscow, then a bus will take them to Star City, where they will be reunited with their families.
"They may go home after seven or 10 days, but they will be able to see their families during this period," Klimuk said.
Tsibliyev, and his wife, son, 20, and daughter, 15, live in Star City. Lazutkin lives near Moscow with his wife and two daughters, one a teenager, the other a toddler.

Vladimir Krivolapov, a doctor on the team, said Tsibliyev, who developed heart trouble due to stress after the worst accident in Mir's history on June 25, would continue to feel under mental pressure. "It will be hard for him psychologically."

President Boris Yeltsin last week said human error may have caused the crash between Mir and a cargo craft Tsibliyev was manoeuvring, the most serious of a string of mishaps which dogged Tsibliyev and Lazutkin's six months in space.

"Even though the guilt for the accident has not been established, public opinion has already been formed," Krivolapov said. "But we don't need to isolate him from news, he would demand that he not be isolated."
